To add, put the numbers together (fàng zài yī-qǐ). To take away, use ná. The answer comes after a comma with shì: shì qī, it's seven.
A describing word right before a noun, with no de, goes with it: lǎo nǚ-rén, an old woman; dà huài dòng-wù, a big bad animal; bié rén, other people.
How or how much someone does it: hěn and a describing word go before the verb.
A number alone can say a number: jīn-nián wǒ èr-shí, this year I am twenty.
Says what you do to a thing: bǎ and the thing come before the action, which ends in a result.
Says what you make a thing be: bǎ, the thing, then a describing word for how it ends up (make the room clean).
Bāng, the person, then the verb: help someone do it. Bāng, the person, then xué and the verb is teach: you help them learn. Hěn huì says someone is good at it.

A noun and a describing word, with no hěn, can describe a place or a thing before de: rén shǎo, zhíwù duō de dì-fāng, a place with few people and many plants; or follow an order: chī shuǐ-guǒ, shēntǐ hǎo.
Says one thing is more than another: bǐ (than) goes between them, then the describing word, with no hěn.
Says something became different: biàn goes before the describing word, and le after it.
Bié before a verb says don't: bié pà, don't be afraid; bié zǒu, don't leave.
Numbers above ten: shí goes before the other number for 11 to 19 (shí-èr) and after it for 20, 30 … (èr-shí). Past ninety-nine, say the digits one by one (yī-líng-líng, 100).
Says something is not so: bù goes before the describing word, with no hěn. Bù hěn means not very.
Says no: bù goes before the verb, shì or the describing word.
Bù before shì says one thing is not another: dòng-wù bù shì zhíwù, an animal is not a plant.
Says part of something: bùfen follows zhè, nà or dà. Dà bùfen before a noun means most of them.
Someone can be called or greeted first, then a comma and what is said: māma, wǒ huí lái le, Mom, I'm back; nǐ hǎo, nǐ shì xué-shēng ma, hello, are you a student?
Néng on its own, or with bù, answers whether something can be done: bù néng, no, you can't.
Says what someone can do: néng goes before the verb, and bù goes before néng for "can't". Kěyǐ means may.
Says how many times: cì goes after hěn duō or duōshǎo, after a number, or after zhè (this time).
After the hour, a number and fēn says the minutes: sān diǎn wǔ fēn, five past three.
Two sentences can be joined with a comma: this one is cold, and that one too.
Says where you come from: cóng goes before the place, then the verb, lái.
Numbers can be said in a row, with commas, and can stand as things themselves: sān bǐ èr duō, three is more than two.
To count kinds, times or parts, put the number before zhǒng, cì or bù-fēn instead of gè: sān-zhǒng, three kinds; yī bù-fēn rén, some of the people.
Dà and xiǎo together name the size: nǐ shēntǐ de dà-xiǎo, the size of your body.
Dàn-shì starts the second part and says but: it looks good, but it does not taste good.
A time word and a number with hào names the date: jīn-tiān shí hào, today is the tenth.
A describing word, or an owner, goes before the noun and takes -de.
A number and diǎn says the hour, and goes before the verb: wǒ sān diǎn huí jiā. An evening or a morning can come first: wǎn-shàng qī diǎn.
What someone does can be the topic of a sentence: xué-xiě bù nán, learning to write isn't hard.
Says they all do it: dōu goes right before the verb, after the people or things. It never goes before a noun.
Say a describing word twice, then -de, to make it stronger and livelier: yuán-yuán-de. No hěn is needed. Before a verb, hǎo-hǎo means well, properly.
Say a counting word, or one of a few nouns, twice for every, and put dōu before the verb: rén-rén dōu, everyone; cì-cì dōu, every time.
Say a verb twice to do it a little or just try it. The second one is short and light: wǒ kàn-kan, let me have a look; xiè-xie, thanks.
Duì on its own says right: nǐ shuō-de duì, what you say is right. Bù duì is wrong; duì-bù-duì asks if it is right.
Duì and a person before a describing word says how someone or something is toward them: tā duì wǒ hěn hǎo. Duì X lái shuō means for X.
Duō before a describing word asks how much: nǐ duō dà, how old are you; duō rè, how hot. Duō-shǎo asks how many or how much.
Hǎo or nán before a verb says it is good or hard to do: hǎo wánr, fun to play; nán zuò, hard to do.
Jué-dé says feel or think, then how it is or a whole thought: wǒ jué-dé hǎo, I feel good; wǒ jué-dé wǒ néng, I think I can. Shuō and yào can take a person and hǎo too: wǒ shuō nǐ hǎo, I say hello.
A feeling can come first, with what it is about right after: hěn kāi-xīn nǐ lái le, I'm so glad you came.
Says something is near: fùjìn goes after zài, or after zài and a place.
Gěi is to give: the person first, then the thing. Before a verb, gěi means for or to: wǒ gěi nǐ xiě, I write to you.
Gěi wǒ and a verb asks for a turn: let me do it. Yī-xià after the verb makes it a quick try.
Says you have done something before: guò goes right after the verb.
Hái-shì gives a choice: A or B? It asks the other person to choose, so it comes in a question.
Says something is still so, or there is more: hái goes before the verb.
A number followed by hào names something by its number: èr-hào, number two. Dì before a number makes it an order: dì-yī, first.
Hǎo ma at the end, after a comma, makes a suggestion or asks nicely: wǒ-men chū-qù wánr, hǎo ma? Hǎo on its own says okay.
Hé joins two nouns: nǐ hé wǒ, you and me. It joins nouns only, not whole sentences.
Hé before a person and a verb says with whom it is done: hé wǒ yī-qǐ wánr, play together with me.
A greeting is someone and hǎo: nǐ hǎo, hello; nǐ-men hǎo, hello to you all; xīn-nián hǎo, happy New Year.
Says what something is like: hěn goes before the describing word.
Says there are many of something: hěn duō goes right before the noun.
Says something will happen: huì goes before the verb.
Jiào, someone, then a verb: tell or have them do it. It works like ràng; bù ràng says you won't let them.
Jiào and a name says what someone is called: wǒ jiào "Lisa", my name is Lisa. Nǐ jiào shénme? asks the name.
Jiù before a number and counting word means only: wǒ jiù yī-gè, I have only one.
Jiù goes right before the verb. After rúguǒ it means then; on its own it means right away or just: wǒ jiù qù, I'm going right away.
Says something starts: kāishǐ goes before the verb.
Says you know how to do something: zhīdào zěnme goes before the verb.
Zhīdào can be followed by a whole sentence: what you know is what happened, or who did it.
Kuài before a verb says hurry or quickly: kuài lái, come quickly. Kuài yào before a verb and le says about to: tā kuài yào lái le, he is about to come.
Wǒ lái and a verb offers to do it: let me. On its own, wǒ lái! means let me!
A span of days, de, and zuì-hòu name its last days: qī tiān de zuì-hòu liǎng tiān, the last two of the seven days.
Says something changed: le goes after the describing word, with no hěn.
Says something is done: le goes right after the verb. The verb itself never changes.
Says something has now happened: le goes at the end of what is said.
Says someone is learning to do something: xué goes before the verb.
Lì-qì, strength-air, is the strength of a body: tā hěn yǒu lì-qì, he is very strong.
Says someone loves doing something: ài goes before the verb.
Asks a yes-or-no question: ma goes at the end of the sentence.
A short yes-or-no question: yǒu … ma, do you have …; yuǎn ma, is it far.
Says it might be so: kěnéng goes before the verb.
A counting word goes after zhè, nà or a number: zhè-ge (this one), zhè-ge rén (this person), liǎng-ge rén (two people).
Méi le says it is gone: wèn-tí jiù méi le, the problem is gone. Wán le says it is used up: shuǐ wán le.
Méi guānxi says never mind: méi guānxi, wǒ bù pà, never mind, I am not afraid.
Méi-yǒu says someone doesn't have a thing: wǒ méi-yǒu jīn, I don't have money. Yǒu is have; méi-yǒu is don't have.
Méi yǒu before the other one and a describing word says not as good as: wǒ méi yǒu tā hǎo, I am not as good as him.
Men after a noun means more than one person: hái-zi-men, the children. After wǒ, nǐ or tā it makes we, you all or they; a number and a counting word can follow: wǒ-men sān-ge rén, the three of us.
Says between or in the middle: zhōng-jiān goes after the places or people.
Xià-gè and shàng-gè before a time word say next and last: xià-gè yuè, next month. Xià yī gè rè-de shí-jiān is next summer.
A verb on its own is an order: chī, eat! For don't, put bù yào first. A countdown ends on the order: yī, èr, sān, kāishǐ!
An owner right before its part says whose part it is, with or without -de: dòng-wù shēntǐ, the animal's body; tā shēntǐ-de wài-miàn, the outside of his body.
Says you hear or see someone do something: tīng or kàn, then who, then what they do.
A place with zài can come first, then the sentence: zài jiā wǒ jué-dé hǎo, at home I feel good.
Says in or on something: lǐ (in) or shàng (on) joins the place.
A number and jīn says how much money: shí jīn, ten; hěn shǎo jīn, very little money.

Says something starts to get that way: qǐ-lái goes after the describing word. After a verb it says how a thing seems when you look, taste or hear it: kàn-qǐ-lái hěn hǎo, it looks good. Xià-qù after a verb says keep going.
Qián and hòu before a counted span of time name the one before or after: qián yī-ge rì is the day before, hòu shí-èr-ge yuè the twelve months after.
Ràng and someone says make or let them: ràng shǒu gānjìng, make the hands clean; ràng tā lái, let him come.
Says you can or can't get the result: dé (can) or bù (can't) goes between the verb and the result.
Rúguǒ starts the if-part, then a comma and the rest: rúguǒ you come, I'll wait for you.
Two actions can follow each other, in the order they happen: zǒu lù qù, walk and go there.
Says everything: shénme-dōu goes before the verb. With bù or méi it means nothing.
Shénme shí-hòu asks when: nǐ shénme shí-hòu lái, when are you coming?
Shénme yánsè asks what color: nǐ-de yīfu shì shénme yánsè? The answer is the color, then de.
Says that one thing is another: shì goes between the two.
An answer can be only what is said: the verb for yes, bù and the verb for no. A sentence can leave the doer out. Shì and bù shì answer alone too, with no complement: yes, it is / no, it isn't.
Shuō bù says no, as an answer or an objection: tā shuō bù, he says no.
A length of time and hòu or qián says how long after or before: sān tiān hòu, in three days.
After shuō, wèn, xiào and other verbs of saying, a colon brings in what was said: tā shuō: nǐ hǎo. What was said runs to the end of the sentence, so its ma or le stays inside it.
Modifiers stack up before one noun, each with its own -de.
A sentence names someone or something, then says something about it.
Who does what to what: the doer, then the action, then what it is done to.
Nà-gè shí-jiān is at that time: nà-gè shí-jiān wǒ zài jiā, at that time I was at home.
Tì before a verb means in someone's place: tā tì wǒ qù, he goes instead of me.

A number goes right before tiān (day) or nián (year), with no gè: sān tiān, three days. How long an action lasts goes after the verb. Míng-tiān (tomorrow), hòu-tiān, qù-nián (last year), míng-nián are times that go first.
Says when: the time comes first, then a comma, then the rest. A time can also stand right after the doer.
To multiply, put a number together many times (fàng zài yī-qǐ sān cì). To divide, say how many times you can take it away (néng ná sān cì).
A thing can come first as the topic, then a whole sentence about it: wǒ bàba shēntǐ hěn hǎo, as for my dad, his body is fine; shénme wǒ dōu yào, whatever it is, I want it.
Asks a yes-or-no question another way: the verb, bù, and the verb again.
To say how someone does something, put -de after the verb and then a describing word: tā shuō de hǎo, he speaks well.
A verb with -de before a noun names the one or the thing that does it: xiě-de rén, the one who writes; wǒ xiě de shū, the book I wrote.
A verb with -de names the thing the action is about: chī-de is food, wǒ xiě de is what I wrote.
Says how an action ends: a result word joins the verb, like kàn-dào (see), zuò-hǎo (fix) or xué-huì (learn until you can).
Says you finished doing something: wán joins the verb, and le follows.
Says "after doing something": hòu goes after the finished action, then a comma and the rest.
Says what someone wants to do: yào (want) or xiǎng (would like) goes before the verb.
Wèi before a person and a verb says for whom: wǒ wèi nǐ zuò le fàn, I cooked for you. Wèi-le starts a reason for doing: wèi-le hái-zi, tā gōng-zuò, for his children he works.
Asks "what?": shénme goes where the answer would go. Before a noun it asks which kind.
Says "when" something happens: say "the time of" it, with -de shíjiān after the action, then a comma.
Nǎ asks which: nǎ-ge rén, which person; nǎ guó rén, from which country; nǎ tiān, which day.
Asks "why?" or "how?": wèi-shénme or zěnme goes before the verb, and wèi-shénme also goes before bù.

How a word shows in writing: the syllables of one word stay together (dòng-wù), a hyphen glues a small word to another so they work as one word (zhè-ge, hěn-dà-de), and quotes mark a name or a sound ("wāng-wāng").
Xià before a thing can mean falls: xià shuǐ, it rains.
Says someone also does it: yě goes right before the verb, after the doer. It also goes before hěn.
Yī diǎn says a little. After a describing word it is a bit more (dà yī diǎn); after yǒu, before a describing word, it is a bit (yǒu yī diǎn lěng); after a verb it is a little of it (chī yī diǎn).
Yī, a verb, jiù and another verb says as soon as: yī kàn jiù zhīdào, you know as soon as you look.
Yī-qǐ before a verb says it is done together: wǒ-men yī-qǐ chī, we eat together.
Yǐ-qián means before and yǐ-hòu means after: yǐ-qián wǒ zài "Zhōngguó", I used to be in China. Xiǎo shí-hòu is as a child; xīn-nián is the New Year.
Says to do something for a moment: yī-xià goes after the verb. It also softens a request.
Says things are the same: yī-yàng goes after the things. Bù yī-yàng says they differ.
Yīnwèi starts the reason: yīnwèi it is cold, I am not going out. The reason can also come second, after a comma.
Yòng and a thing before a verb says what you do it with: wǒ yòng gōng-jù xiě, I write with a tool.
Says something happens again: yòu goes before the verb, and le after it.
Yǒu-xiē before a noun means some: yǒu-xiē rén bù lái, some people aren't coming.
Says something is happening right now: zài goes before the verb, like -ing in English.
Says where someone or something is: zài goes before the place. A place can also come before the verb: where it is done.
Zěnme-yàng asks how it is: jīn-tiān zěnme yàng, how is today.
Zhè-yàng before a verb says in this way: nǐ zhè-yàng zuò, do it like this.
Says really: zhēn goes before the describing word. On its own it is a whole sentence.
Says only: zhǐ goes before the verb.
Says the most: zuì goes before the describing word or the verb. Zuì-hòu is last.
Says you make something so: zuò goes before the result. Zuò hǎo is fix it, zuò huài is break it.
